first.rationale: The competitor's entry pricing creates pressure to match with promotional_pricing, but memory_73 is explicit that discounting materially reduced 30-day retention and should not be generalized; matching price would trade the primary objective (sustainable long-term qualified revenue) for a short-term acquisition bump. The two metrics actually degrading are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and both memory_31 (signup simplification -> durable SMB activation lift) and memory_86 (shorter onboarding -> completion and time-to-value lift) point at the same lever, which also indirectly defends against price-sensitive churn by getting accounts to value faster. I am verifying memory_31 and memory_86 rather than memories supporting directions I am not taking, because those two are the records I would actually be acting on, and both are consolidated summaries whose original records may have carried caveats that were stripped during consolidation. Note that memory_73 is the only inherited memory that retained a downstream-harm caveat; the others report only upside metrics, which is more plausibly a gap in what was recorded than evidence that no downstream cost exists. So I treat memory_31/86 as directional, not settled. Referral_incentive (memory_57) targets established customers and does not address the observed declines; enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) is a different segment from the one under attack. Running as a standard experiment with a holdout, instrumented for 30- and 60-day retention and qualified-revenue quality, not just completion/activation rates, so we do not repeat the promotional-pricing pattern of a strong headline lift masking downstream value loss. If verification shows memory_31 or memory_86 measured only short-horizon funnel metrics, I will narrow to a small guarded test.
